title: Black and Latin American people, those with low-incomes, less likely to have a family doctor: report
summary: We often hear about people struggling to find a family doctor, but a new report from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows the difficulty can vary depending on your age and race.

image.caption: A new report by the Canadian Institute for Health Information says that while 83 per cent of adults and 89 per cent of children and youth have a primary-care provider, access is much poorer for racialized and low-income individuals. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Health·New
We often hear about people struggling to find a family doctor, but a new report from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows the difficulty can vary depending on your age and race.
About 6 million people in Canada lack a primary-care provider, like a family doctor or nurse practitioner
We often hear about people struggling to find a family doctor, but a new report says the difficulty can vary depending on your age and race.

The report, released Wednesday by the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI), also found that adults with the lowest incomes were less likely to have a primary-care provider, such a family doctor or nurse practitioner, than those with the highest incomes — 78 per cent compared to 87 per cent.
It also found that Black and Latin American adults were less likely (66 and 68 per cent, respectively) to have a provider than white adults (86 per cent).

Most Canadians have a primary-care provider — 83 per cent of adults and 89 per cent of children and youth according to Babita Gupta, the report's lead author. But the report notes that leaves some six million who do not.
However, having a primary-care provider "doesn't guarantee timely access to care," Gupta, who is CIHI's manager of health system analytics, told CBC News.
"Only 26 per cent received same-day or next-day care when they needed it," during the report's 12-month period, she said.
Gupta says adults aged 18 to 34 are less likely to have a regular provider, but the most likely to get a same- or next-day appointment.
Family physician and researcher Dr. Tara Kiran points out the report did not examine access among Indigenous people, who are known to face some of the biggest barriers. (CBC)
"The reason is because they were possibly able to access care through walk-in clinics or through other means."
The downside to that, says Dr. Tara Kiran, a family doctor and researcher at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto, is that walk-ins don't follow or co-ordinate someone's care over time.
Poorer access to primary care among lower-income individuals may be linked to their ability to get to a clinic, says Kiran, who was not involved in the report.
"They're often working Monday to Friday, nine to five, and it's hard to take time off that work and doctors' offices are often not providing routine care in the evenings or on weekends."
The report also found that in lower-income neighbourhoods people are more likely to be hospitalized for things like diabetes and high blood pressure. (Doug Ives/The Canadian Press)
The report also found that in the lowest-income neighbourhoods, hospitalizations for things like diabetes and high blood pressure are three times higher.
Kiran says she wasn't surprised to see the report's finding that, for example, members of the Black community were less likely to have a family doctor.

"We know that people who are Black or racialized, they often don't feel culturally safe sometimes in a clinical setting, especially if that clinical setting doesn't include health professionals that reflect their own background," she said.
Kiran also points out that the report is clear that it does not include the experiences of Indigenous people, "but it's the group that actually faces some of the biggest barriers."

blocks.text: While the report does not get into the reasons why Black and Latin American people have less access to primary-care providers, Kiran says one factor could be that many people in those groups are newer to Canada.
"That adds a different dimension in terms of access to care," Kiran said. "Many of them don't know how to navigate our system, understandably."
Even with those gaps, Kiran says she was happy to read the report's finding that about seven in 10 people who have a regular provider say they're satisfied.
"We know that there's lots of people who are doing good work."
She says while progress is being made, big hurdles remain.
